DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

**What the paper proposes.** Raise the prices of fish and chips, the burger and the sirloin steak. Replace the mushroom risotto with a seasonal vegetarian special. It projects £810 a week (£42,120 a year) of extra gross profit and a main-course margin of about 71%, and plans eight weeks of monitoring.

**The verdict in brief.** The data gathering is good, and most of the paper's arithmetic is correct. Two problems change the picture:
- The risotto recommendation contradicts the paper's own table.
- The profit projection ignores the beef price rise that the paper itself reports.

The price increases may still be worth making, but for a smaller gain than claimed.

---

## 1. What checks out

- **The table's margins.** Every figure in Table 1 is correct. Fish 69%, burger 72%, curry 75%, steak 60% and risotto 80%. Plates total 1,050 a week.
- **The £810 arithmetic.** £310 + £260 + £240 = £810, and × 52 = £42,120.
- **The midpoint claim.** All three new prices are below the competitor midpoints: £17.50 vs about £17.98, £16.00 vs £16.50, and £28.00 vs £29.50.
- **The 71% figure, taken on its own assumptions.** Main-course margin is currently about 69–70% and would reach about 71%. This ignores the beef rise (see §3).

---

## 2. The risotto: the paper's own table says the opposite

Section 5.2 says the risotto "has the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows it has the **highest**, at 80%.

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** | **£11.20** |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |

- **In cash terms it isn't weak either.** Each risotto earns more than a burger or a curry. Together, its 90 plates make about £1,000 of gross profit a week.
- **"Lowest sales" is only half true.** At 90 plates it ties with the specials.
- **The replacement probably earns less.** Specials currently run at a 64% margin. A special at £14 with that margin earns about £8.96 a plate, roughly £2.24 less than the risotto. Over 90 plates that is about **£200 a week less gross profit, or around £10,000 a year.** The paper doesn't count this, and it would also pull down the 71% margin.
- **The menu would lose its permanent vegetarian main.** The risotto appears to be the only one. A rotating special may work less well for regulars, and for groups where one diner is vegetarian and decides where the group eats.

Section 5.2 should be dropped unless there are reasons for it that the paper doesn't give.

---

## 3. The projection leaves out the beef price rise

Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day as the new prices. Section 5.3 still holds food costs at January–February levels.

If the whole plate cost of the burger and steak rose 12%:

| Dish | Extra cost per plate | Plates a week | Extra cost a week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | about £0.50 | 260 | about £131 |
| Steak | about £1.25 | 120 | about £150 |
| **Total** | | | **about £281** |

This is an upper bound, because buns, chips and sides won't rise. Even so, most of the burger and steak increases simply pass the beef rise on to customers. The paper presents them as new profit. With the beef rise included, main-course margin stays roughly where it is now, about 69–70%. It does not reach 71%.

---

## 4. VAT: worth confirming

UK menu prices normally include 20% VAT, and a business with sales this large is certainly VAT-registered. If so, each £1 rise brings in £0.83, not £1. The table's margins are also calculated on prices that include VAT. Applying both corrections:

| Dish | Gross profit per plate now (excl. VAT) | After rise and beef increase | Gain per plate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £8.65 | £9.48 | +£0.83 |
| Beef burger | £8.30 | £8.63 | +£0.33 |
| Sirloin steak | £11.27 | £11.68 | +£0.42 |

That comes to about **£390 a week, or around £20,000 a year**, before the risotto swap. Without the VAT correction, the beef rise alone brings the figure down to about £530 a week (£27,500 a year). Either way, it is well below £42,000.

If the restaurant already calculates gross profit on prices excluding VAT, this correction doesn't apply. The owners should check which basis the 70% target uses.

**Most of the real gain comes from fish and chips.** The burger and steak increases leave little room. Once VAT and beef are included, sales of either would only need to **fall about 4%** to wipe out the gain on that dish. "If volumes hold" is therefore the assumption everything depends on. "Low-risk" overstates the position.

---

## 5. Pricing position and customer response

- **The restaurant stops being the cheapest.** All three dishes are currently the lowest-priced in the comparison group. After the rises, every one is above the cheapest competitor (£16.95, £15.50 and £27.00). "Below the midpoint" is accurate, but "we remain the value option" is a weaker claim.
- **Loyalty doesn't mean customers won't notice prices.** Repeat guests are the ones most likely to notice the change, since they know the old prices. A 60% share of bookings from repeat guests doesn't show they will accept higher prices.
- **The 2024 comparison is weak evidence.** "No visible effect on bookings" isn't measured. Bookings also miss changes in what people order, such as fewer steaks or fewer extra dishes.
- **The lunch share isn't shown.** Lunch trade is called small, but Friday and Saturday dinner make up just under half of mains. The rest is never broken down.

---

## 6. Monitoring

- **The baseline will mislead.** January–February is usually the quietest period. Spring trade will probably rise anyway, which could hide falling sales. Compare with April–May 2025 instead, or set an expected seasonal uplift in advance.
- **There is no trigger.** An early warning needs a threshold agreed in advance, for example "if steak plates fall more than 5% against seasonal expectation, review."
- **Plates per dish are only part of the picture.** Also track covers, spend per head, and shifts in what people order, such as steak customers switching to curry.

---

## 7. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** Section 8 says "six trading days a week," but section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. This doesn't affect the weekly figures but should be corrected.
- **Price only.** Competitors were compared on price alone, not portion size or quality. That's acceptable for this paper but worth acknowledging.

---

## Bottom line

- **Price increases.** Probably still sensible, mainly because beef costs are rising. Present them honestly: the burger and steak rises mostly pass on the beef increase, and the real gain, chiefly from fish and chips, is roughly £20,000–28,000 a year depending on how VAT is treated. Margin stays around 69–70%, not 71%.
- **Risotto.** Keep it. The paper's own data show it is the highest-margin main.
- **Monitoring.** Use a seasonal baseline and set a trigger in advance.
- **Still open.** How customers respond to the price rises. The monitoring, fixed as above, is what will answer that.
